Note that

[MATH: \mathbf F(t)=\int \mathbf F'(t)\, \textrm d t=\int \left\langle 6t^5+2t,\, \sec^2 t\right\rangle \, \textrm d t.]

[MATH: ∫⟨6t^{5} + 2t, \sec^{2} t⟩dt|= ⟨∫(6t^{5} + 2t)dt, ∫\sec^{2} tdt⟩; = ⟨t^{6} + t^{2} + c_{1}, \tan t + c_{2}⟩; = ⟨t^{6} + t^{2}, \tan t⟩ + ⟨c_{1}, c_{2}⟩; = ⟨t^{6} + t^{2}, \tan t⟩ + C,]

where [MATH: \mathbf C] is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

sections.normalized_html:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

[MATH: ∫⟨\cos (2t + 1), 4⟩dt = ⟨∫\cos (2t + 1)dt, ∫4dt⟩.]

  • For [MATH: x(t) =\cos(2t+1),] we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let [MATH: u= 2t +1.] Then
    [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d t} = 2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d t = \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u.] Therefore, we have [MATH: ∫x(t)dt|= ∫\cos (2t + 1)dt; = ∫\cos u ⋅ (1)/(2)du; = (1)/(2)∫\cos udu; = (1)/(2)(\sin u) + c_{1}; = (1)/(2)\sin (2t + 1) + c_{1}.]

  • For [MATH: y(t) =4,] we have [MATH: ∫y(t)dt = ∫4dt = 4t + c_{2}.]

Finally, we have

[MATH: ∫⟨\cos (2t + 1), 4⟩dt|= ⟨(1)/(2)\sin (2t + 1) + c_{1}, 4t + c_{2}⟩; = ⟨(1)/(2)\sin (2t + 1), 4t⟩ + ⟨c_{1}, c_{2}⟩; = ⟨(1)/(2)\sin (2t + 1), 4t⟩ + C.]

sections.normalized_html:
Note that

[MATH: \mathbf F(t)=\int \mathbf F'(t)\, \textrm d t=\int \left\langle \sec t \tan t,\, \sin(2t)\right\rangle \, \textrm d t.]

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

[MATH: ∫⟨\sec t\tan t, \sin (2t)⟩dt|= ⟨∫\sec t\tan tdt, ∫\sin (2t)dt⟩; = ⟨\sec t + c_{1}, − (1)/(2)\cos (2t) + c_{2}⟩.]

The initial condition [MATH: \mathbf F(0)=\left\langle 0,\, 0 \right\rangle] gives

[MATH: F(0) = ⟨\sec 0 + c_{1}, − (1)/(2)\cos (2 ⋅ 0) + c_{2}⟩|= ⟨0, 0⟩; ⟨1 + c_{1}, − (1)/(2) + c_{2}⟩|= ⟨0, 0⟩.]

Therefore, [MATH: c_1=-1] and [MATH: c_2=\dfrac 12.] Consequently,

[MATH: \mathbf F(t)=\left\langle \sec t - 1 , \, -\dfrac 1 2\cos(2t)+ \dfrac12\right\rangle.]
